nlm-b1-first-notebook-sources.q: You upload a scanned PDF policy manual to a new Claude Project, and it shows as uploaded with no visible error. What's the real risk here?
options: The Project will automatically reject the file after 24 hours
A scanned, image-only PDF with no selectable text layer may yield little or no usable content, without any obvious error
Claude will convert it to audio automatically
The file will count double against the per-chat file limit
nlm-b1-first-notebook-sources.why: Uploading scanned or image-only PDFs and assuming Claude extracted the full text is a listed common mistake — Claude can extract little or nothing from them while the upload still appears to have succeeded.

nlm-b1-first-notebook-sources.q: After adding three files to a new Claude Project, what should you do before asking your first real question?
options: Immediately ask a broad open-ended question to test the Project
Run an inventory-style prompt asking Claude to summarize what each file contributes and flag any gaps or failed uploads
Delete two of the three files to simplify the Project
Wait 24 hours for background indexing before doing anything
nlm-b1-first-notebook-sources.why: The inventory-check prompt forces Claude to account for every file individually, surfacing a failed-to-parse or redundant file in minute two instead of an hour later.

nlm-b1-first-notebook-sources.q: You set up a Claude Project but skip writing custom instructions. What's the practical consequence?
options: Claude will refuse to answer any questions until instructions are added
Claude may quietly blend general knowledge in with the uploaded files instead of sticking to them
The Project automatically deletes itself after a week
File uploads are disabled without custom instructions
nlm-b1-first-notebook-sources.why: Skipping custom instructions is a listed common mistake — unlike a source-locked tool, Claude doesn't default to answering only from uploaded files; it will blend in general knowledge unless explicitly restricted.

nlm-b2-grounded-questions-citations.q: You ask Claude a question inside your Project and get a fluent, confident-sounding answer. What's the core habit this lesson wants you to build?
options: Trust the answer since Claude only uses your uploaded files by default
Require Claude to quote its exact source sentence and file name, then open that file yourself to verify it
Ask the same question in a new Project to cross-check
Only trust answers that don't include any quotes
nlm-b2-grounded-questions-citations.why: Claude has no automatic citation-chip panel like a dedicated grounded tool — the trust mechanism has to be requiring verbatim quotes with a named source, then personally verifying them against the original file.

nlm-b2-grounded-questions-citations.q: You ask Claude to quote its source and it gives you wording that looks slightly off from what you remember the document saying. What should you do?
options: Trust it, since Claude wouldn't invent a quote
Open the original file and search for the exact quoted text to confirm it's accurate and not a paraphrase presented as a quote
Assume the source file itself was edited
Ask a different question instead
nlm-b2-grounded-questions-citations.why: Treating a paraphrase as an exact quote is a listed common mistake — since Claude has no automatic passage-highlighting, opening the file and searching for the quoted text yourself is the only reliable check.

nlm-b2-grounded-questions-citations.q: You deliberately ask your Project a question about a topic none of your files cover. What's the correct behavior to look for?
options: Claude should answer confidently using general knowledge to fill the gap
Claude should say the files don't address this rather than quietly answering from outside knowledge
Claude should refuse to answer any further questions in that Project
Claude should delete the unanswerable question from the chat history
nlm-b2-grounded-questions-citations.why: This is a deliberate test of whether custom instructions are actually holding — Claude should plainly state the gap rather than quietly blending in general knowledge.

nlm-i1-synthesize-multiple-documents.q: You have four vendor proposal files in a Project with different pricing figures and ask Claude to "summarize all of this." What's the likely problem with this prompt?
options: It will refuse since four files exceed some limit
It tends to blend files into one voice, losing track of which file said what and potentially averaging conflicting numbers
It only works if all four documents are the same file type
It will only summarize the first file uploaded
nlm-i1-synthesize-multiple-documents.why: A lazy 'summarize all of this' prompt tends to blend files into mush, and this is exactly the failure mode where numeric disagreement gets silently averaged or resolved rather than surfaced.

nlm-i1-synthesize-multiple-documents.q: Why does the structured synthesis prompt explicitly forbid Claude from averaging or picking one number when files disagree on pricing?
options: Averaging is computationally expensive for the model
Silently resolving a real disagreement into one plausible number is the exact danger the prompt is designed to prevent
Claude cannot perform arithmetic on numbers from different files
Averages are only allowed on certain Claude plans
nlm-i1-synthesize-multiple-documents.why: Explicitly forbidding averaging or picking a winner stops Claude from doing the one thing that makes multi-document synthesis dangerous: quietly resolving a disagreement into a single blended figure.

nlm-i1-synthesize-multiple-documents.q: After getting a structured agreement/disagreement/unique-points synthesis, what should you specifically do with the disagreement section before using it?
options: Accept it as-is since it already separates agreement from disagreement
Open the named files yourself to confirm Claude quoted the conflicting figures accurately
Delete the disagreement section since it adds complexity
Ask Claude to pick which file is correct for you
nlm-i1-synthesize-multiple-documents.why: Accepting flagged disagreements without opening the named files to confirm Claude read them correctly is a listed common mistake — verification is required before you rely on the attribution.

nlm-i2-study-system-course-materials.q: A student uploads an entire semester's worth of materials into one Gemini conversation, then asks for a practice quiz. What goes wrong?
options: Gemini won't accept that many files in one conversation
The generated quiz and study guide end up mixing content from unrelated units instead of staying scoped to what's being tested next
Gemini automatically archives older units
Flashcard-style questions can no longer be generated
nlm-i2-study-system-course-materials.why: Uploading an entire semester's materials into one conversation is a listed common mistake; starting one conversation per course unit keeps generated study material scoped to what's actually being tested next.

nlm-i2-study-system-course-materials.q: You miss a practice question on mitochondria vs. chloroplast function. What's the most effective next step according to the lesson?
options: Re-read the same flashcard-style card that already covers this topic
Use the targeted follow-up prompt to get an explanation grounded in the uploaded material and a genuinely new question testing real understanding
Regenerate the entire study guide from scratch
Skip the topic since it's a minor detail
nlm-i2-study-system-course-materials.why: Asking Gemini to point to exactly where the material covers it forces you back to the real reading rather than trusting a possibly-imprecise flashcard, and asking for a genuinely new follow-up question checks understanding instead of pattern-matched recall.

nlm-i2-study-system-course-materials.q: After generating flashcard-style Q&A pairs from your uploaded course materials, why does the lesson recommend spot-checking a handful against the actual reading?
options: Flashcards expire after 24 hours if unverified
There's no built-in review step in Gemini, so an occasional flattened nuance can slip through unnoticed
Spot-checking is required to unlock the practice quiz
It reduces the number of files counted in the conversation
nlm-i2-study-system-course-materials.why: The lesson warns that with no built-in review step, generated flashcards can occasionally flatten an important nuance, so spot-checking a sample against the real reading is part of the workflow.

nlm-i3-briefings-summaries-for-work.q: A generated briefing ends up re-summarizing every file in full instead of focusing on what leadership needs to decide. What went wrong?
options: The Project's file panel malfunctioned
The briefing was allowed to balloon into a full re-summary instead of being scoped to what the specific audience needs to act on
Too few files were uploaded to the Project
Claude doesn't support audience-specific prompts
nlm-i3-briefings-summaries-for-work.why: Letting the briefing balloon into a full re-summary of every file instead of only what the audience needs to act on is a listed common mistake — a briefing is not a re-summary of the whole Project.

nlm-i3-briefings-summaries-for-work.q: Why does the briefing prompt explicitly instruct Claude not to add outside context or unsupported recommendations?
options: It speeds up generation time
It guards against Claude padding gaps with plausible-sounding but unsourced claims, which matters most when readers act without checking the files themselves
It's a formatting requirement with no substantive effect
It's required to enable the Artifact feature
nlm-i3-briefings-summaries-for-work.why: Requiring a quote on every fact and forbidding outside context guards against Claude filling gaps with unsupported claims — critical because the audience will act on the briefing without checking the source files themselves.

nlm-i3-briefings-summaries-for-work.q: The generated briefing includes a section titled "open questions the files don't resolve." Why does the lesson say to keep this section rather than trim it out?
options: It's required by Claude's Artifact format and can't be removed
It's often more useful to a stakeholder than the summary itself, since it tells them exactly what still needs to be found out
It reduces the number of quotes needed
It's only relevant for legal audiences
nlm-i3-briefings-summaries-for-work.why: The lesson's proTip explicitly notes that the open-questions section is often more useful to a stakeholder than the summary, because it tells them precisely what still needs to be found out.

nlm-a1-client-project-knowledge-base.q: A consultant juggling three clients considers using one shared Claude Project for all of them to save setup time. What's the actual risk?
options: Claude will merge the clients' billing automatically
Mixing multiple clients' documents risks Claude blending context between engagements in an answer, a confidentiality risk
Shared Projects have a lower file limit than single-client ones
Nothing — Claude automatically isolates each client's files
nlm-a1-client-project-knowledge-base.why: Mixing multiple clients' documents into one Project is a listed common mistake — it risks Claude blending context between engagements, which matters especially for confidentiality-sensitive work.

nlm-a1-client-project-knowledge-base.q: A client engagement Project now has SOW v1 and v2, with old call transcripts still referencing terms from v1. What convention prevents confusion here?
options: Deleting all transcripts once a new SOW version is uploaded
A clear naming/versioning convention (v1, v2, final, date-stamped) so it's obvious which document is currently authoritative
Merging all versions into a single combined file before uploading
Creating a brand new Project for every SOW revision
nlm-a1-client-project-knowledge-base.why: Establishing a naming convention for files — date-stamping notes and labeling draft versions clearly — makes it obvious which document is currently authoritative, avoiding the risk of quoting a stale draft.

nlm-a1-client-project-knowledge-base.q: Before a client meeting, the meeting-prep prompt is run against the Project and returns a contradiction between a recent transcript and the current SOW version. Why does the prompt ask Claude to flag this rather than silently pick one?
options: Because Claude can't process more than one file version at a time
Because without being told to prefer recency and flag conflicts, Claude may silently answer from whichever version it reads first
Because flagging conflicts is required to stay under a plan's file limit
Because contradictions always indicate a corrupted file
nlm-a1-client-project-knowledge-base.why: Without explicit instruction to prefer recency and flag contradictions, Claude may silently answer from whichever version it happens to read first — exactly the failure mode a living knowledge base needs to avoid.

nlm-a2-compare-reconcile-conflicting-sou.q: Two contract draft files in a Project have different liability caps ($50,000 vs $250,000). You ask Claude to "compare these." What's the risk with that generic phrasing?
options: Claude will refuse to compare legal documents
It tends to quietly synthesize one blended answer, hiding exactly the disagreement you need to see
It will only compare the two files' formatting, not content
It requires a higher-tier plan to compare more than one file
nlm-a2-compare-reconcile-conflicting-sou.why: A generic 'compare these' question tends to quietly blend conflicting files into one plausible-sounding but wrong composite, hiding the real disagreement.

nlm-a2-compare-reconcile-conflicting-sou.q: The reconciliation prompt asks Claude to categorize each disagreement as factual, numeric, interpretive, or scope/emphasis. Why does this categorization matter?
options: It's purely cosmetic formatting for the output
It distinguishes real contradictions from differences where both files are correct but simply talking about different things
It determines which file gets deleted from the Project
It's required before Claude will quote a source
nlm-a2-compare-reconcile-conflicting-sou.why: Confusing a scope or emphasis difference — where both files are correct but discussing different things — with a genuine contradiction is a listed common mistake; explicit categorization prevents that confusion.

nlm-a2-compare-reconcile-conflicting-sou.q: Claude surfaces a disagreement between two forecasts but doesn't say which one is correct, even though asked to rank by importance. Is this expected behavior?
options: No, it's a malfunction — it should always pick the more likely correct file
Yes, the prompt deliberately withholds a verdict since resolving which file is right is the user's professional judgment call
No, ranking by importance requires it to also declare a winner
Yes, but only because both files are equally low quality
nlm-a2-compare-reconcile-conflicting-sou.why: The prompt explicitly instructs Claude not to declare which claim is correct — that judgment call belongs to the human, and Claude's job is only to surface, quote, and categorize the disagreement.

nlm-a3-advanced-team-knowledge-workflows.q: Several teammates each build their own separate Gem covering the same onboarding topic. What's the problem with this pattern?
options: Gemini will merge them automatically after a week
It's a listed common mistake — without one canonical, owned Gem, the knowledge workflow fragments and goes stale since no one owns the source folder
Personal Gems can't use Deep Research
It exceeds the per-user Gem count limit
nlm-a3-advanced-team-knowledge-workflows.why: Letting every team member build their own version of the same Gem or document instead of maintaining one canonical, owned version is a listed common mistake — it lacks the single owner responsible for keeping the source folder current.

nlm-a3-advanced-team-knowledge-workflows.q: A team lead turns on Deep Research's Workspace sources without checking what it can actually access. What does the lesson warn about this?
options: It's always safe since Workspace sources never surface unexpected content
Turning it on without checking what it can access risks being surprised by what it surfaces
Workspace sources require a paid plan and shouldn't be used casually
Deep Research ignores Workspace sources by default and this setting does nothing
nlm-a3-advanced-team-knowledge-workflows.why: Turning on Deep Research's Workspace sources without checking what it can actually access, and being surprised by what it surfaces, is a listed common mistake.

nlm-a3-advanced-team-knowledge-workflows.q: A team's shared Gem and Drive folder haven't been reviewed in months. What should happen per the lesson?
options: Nothing — Gems never go stale once created
Set a review cadence for the Gem and its source folder, the same way you'd review a live automation, so stale files get pruned
Delete the Gem and have everyone go back to individual uploads
Ignore staleness since Deep Research always pulls the latest web content anyway
nlm-a3-advanced-team-knowledge-workflows.why: The lesson calls for setting a review cadence for the shared Gem and its source folder, the same way you'd review a live automation, so the team keeps trusting it rather than letting it go stale.
